_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-16) cold case update reads 5 months later, so 2 March falls inside it (the night is 31 October)
title: Build or Buy
setting: a bowling alley's late league night

post.author: u/lane_lights_pegeen
post.title: I run the night desk at a bowling alley. On league night all 24 lanes went dark mid-frame for 9 minutes, and the log says none of them had paid. Every one had.

blocks.text: I'm Pegeen, night duty manager at a 24-lane bowling alley. We open noon to 23:00, every day of the year. Saturday is league night: teams bowl against each other until closing, every lane booked and paid.

The machine at the end of each lane that sweeps and sets the pins, the pinsetter, and its score screen run only while the lane is paid. A box behind my desk checks that in steps: once a minute, on the minute, it asks the booking system's records whether each lane is paid. Yes: the lane stays on. No, or no answer: the lane is marked unpaid and switched off. That box is the lane controller.

The booking system keeps every booking in an organised store of records that programs can ask questions, like a card index that answers back: a database. On Friday 29 August 2025, fourteen months ago, Meinir, our founder and owner, had a contractor set it up so a company runs it for us on its own computers, for a monthly fee: a managed database.
The company rents out computers in buildings we never see: a cloud provider. It does the chores: it keeps spare copies of our records and installs updates, fixes to the software underneath.

Updates come in a weekly half hour when the provider may take the database offline: the maintenance window. It goes in steps. Someone picks its hour, or the provider picks one at random. The provider emails a notice. An update marked required carries an apply date; after that date, it runs in the next window.

The contractor left every setting as it came: one copy of the database, in one zone, one of the provider's buildings near London. A second copy kept up to date in another zone can take over: if the first stops answering, the provider switches to it. That's a standby copy. We have none.
Tonight, Saturday 31 October 2026, was league night, in costume. The clocks went back last Sunday. At 22:31, mid-frame, every lane went dark.
Twenty-four pinsetters froze with their sweeps down, and twenty-four screens went black over a hall of masks.

The league shouted. Elffin, our mechanic, checked the machines: nothing wrong. The controller's screen said "booking database: no answer". At 22:40 every lane came back by itself. The controller's log; each line is the time, the lanes, the database's answer, and what the controller did:

22:30  lanes 1-24  paid       on
22:31  lanes 1-24  no answer  unpaid, off
22:32  lanes 1-24  no answer  unpaid, off
...
22:39  lanes 1-24  no answer  unpaid, off
22:40  lanes 1-24  paid       on

Meinir later sent me the provider's login. Its page keeps UTC, the world's reference clock: ours match it in winter, an hour ahead in summer. It lists tonight's update to the operating system, the base program a computer runs: "required, apply date Monday 26 October 2026", 22:31 to 22:40 UTC.

It lists two earlier required updates, Saturday 20 September 2025 and Saturday 13 June 2026, both 22:31 to 22:40 UTC, and none between. Nothing went dark either night. Our window: "Saturday 22:30 UTC, assigned". Tonight's notice went on Tuesday 29 September 2026 to Meinir's old work address.

blocks.label: league_night_2231.png

diagram.aria: Saturday 31 October 2026, 22:25 to 22:45 local, which tonight is also UTC. The provider's maintenance window is open from 22:30. The booking database answers until 22:31, is offline from 22:31 to 22:40, and answers again from 22:40. The 24 lanes are lit until 22:31, dark and marked unpaid from 22:31 to 22:40, and lit again from 22:40. Markers: 22:30 window opens, 22:31 update starts, 22:40 back.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the controller's log and the provider's page, Saturday 31 October 2026. Since the clocks went back on Sunday 25 October, our clocks and UTC read the same. The window opened at 22:30, the update began one minute in, at 22:31, and the only copy was offline until 22:40. The controller checks once a minute, on the minute, so the checks from 22:31 to 22:39 got no answer: 9 minutes dark, 24 lanes × 9 = 216 lane-minutes marked unpaid. All 24 lanes were paid until 23:00.

blocks.text: Nothing in our building broke. Everything obeyed something we've never seen. What should we change before next Saturday's league?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Three questions. On those two summer Saturdays, what did your own clocks say at 22:31 UTC, and where were your bowlers? When the controller can't check, what does it decide, and who chose that? And how many copies of the database were answering at 22:31 tonight?

replies.author: u/lane_lights_pegeen
replies.text: In summer we run an hour ahead, so 22:31 UTC was 23:31 here, half an hour after we lock up. Tonight it was 22:31 here. When it can't check, the controller says unpaid; nobody chose that, it came that way. And one copy. 24 lanes × 9 minutes = 216 lane-minutes marked unpaid.

comments.author: u/they_handle_it_peredur
comments.text: Managed means they handle it. That's what Meinir pays for. Find the setting for the provider's updates, switch them off for weekends and forget about it. Your lanes ran fourteen months without a blink; one update on league night is the only thing that has ever gone wrong.

comments.author: u/own_box_sulien
comments.text: I'd never rent the thing my lanes depend on. Put a server, a computer whose job is answering other machines' questions, in your back office and run the database on it yourselves. Then nobody touches it on a Saturday unless you say so.

replies.author: u/lane_lights_pegeen
replies.text: Elffin asked who goes to it when its storage fills up at 3 AM. I didn't have an answer.

reply.prompt: Next Saturday is league night again, all 24 lanes booked and paid until 23:00. What should the alley change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Turn off the provider's updates for the booking database, so none land on a Saturday.
options.part2: On Monday 2 November 2026 Meinir found the setting and switched updates off. It stopped the optional ones. In the sim, set updates to "off" and play the night again: the required update still starts at 22:31, and the lanes are dark until 22:40, 216 lane-minutes marked unpaid, because its apply date had passed. That is what happened next. In February another required update was announced, and its notice went to Meinir's old address like the others. On Saturday 6 March 2027, still winter, at 22:31, all 24 lanes went dark mid-frame again, for 9 minutes, in front of the same league.
options.senior: A managed database's updates are not one switch. Optional ones can wait for ever; required ones, mostly security and reliability fixes, carry an apply date, and after it the provider applies them in the next window whatever your setting says. Even where an update can be held back, holding back security fixes on the system that takes your money is a risk of its own. "Managed means they handle it" is half true: the provider handles doing the update, and you still own when it lands, how many copies are answering when it does, and who reads the notice.

options.text: Run the booking database on our own server in the back office, and update it ourselves.
options.part2: Through November the contractor moved the bookings onto a server in the back office, and Saturdays went quiet. In the sim, with our own server: no provider window, 0 minutes dark. But the chores the alley owns went from 3 to 5: settings, updates, backups, failover, the 3 AM disk alarm. Updates waited for the contractor's visits. On Tuesday 19 January 2027 at 03:00 the server's storage filled up, its alarm rang on Meinir's phone, and nobody knew what was safe to delete. At noon we opened on paper bookings, with Elffin switching lanes on by hand.
options.senior: Self-hosting is a real choice, not a mistake: you decide every moment of downtime, and no notice can go astray. The price is that every chore the provider did becomes yours: applying updates promptly, taking and testing backups, building your own second copy and its switch-over, and someone who answers an alarm at 3 AM. For an alley with no engineer on staff, that swaps vendor risk for staff risk, the risk of one person, one laptop, one missed night. It pays off when you have the people and a reason the provider can't meet, such as a rule about where data must live.

options.text: Move the booking database to another cloud provider, one with a better record.
options.part2: The contractor spent until Christmas moving the bookings: exporting the records, loading them into the new provider's database, and changing how the lane controller connects. The new database came, again, with one copy and no window chosen, so the new provider picked one at random: Saturday 22:10 UTC. In the sim, choose another provider's window and play: dark 22:11 to 22:20, 216 lane-minutes marked unpaid. On Saturday 13 February 2027 its first required update did exactly that, during the league's winter final.
options.senior: Every managed database has maintenance, because every one runs on software that needs fixes; a better record does not remove windows, it moves them. Moving also costs you: the export, the new connection details, the testing, the weeks of the contractor's time. That cost is lock-in, and it grows the longer you stay. Leaving a provider is worth planning as an exit, but it is not a fix for settings you never changed. The new building came with the same defaults as the old one, and the same Saturday-night arithmetic.

options.text: Keep the managed database, add a standby copy, and pick a quiet maintenance hour.
options.part2: On Monday 2 November 2026 Meinir and the contractor changed three settings and one rule. The window is now Tuesday 10:00 UTC: 10:00 here in winter, 11:00 in summer, both before our noon opening. A standby copy runs in a second zone. The provider's notices go to the duty managers' shared inbox, read every shift. And the controller now keeps a lane on its last confirmed booking for up to 15 minutes when no answer comes. In the sim, with all four: 0 minutes dark, two copies answering. With the old Saturday window and the standby: switch-over at 22:40:10 for 40 seconds, between two checks, 0 dark. The next required update ran on Tuesday 12 January 2027 at 10:01 UTC, to an empty hall.
options.senior: Keep what the provider does well, the updates, the spare copies and the switch-over machinery, and take back what was always yours: its settings, its notices and your exit plan. A window chosen for your quietest hour, in UTC, checked against both your summer and your winter clocks, puts planned work where nobody bowls. A standby in a second zone turns an operating-system update into a switch-over of under a minute. A fallback on the lanes, the last confirmed booking for up to 15 minutes, covers that minute and anything like it. Each part covers a different failure; none of them needs a new provider or a server in the back office.

sim.title: Replay league night, 31 October 2026
sim.lede: You're Pegeen, replaying Saturday 31 October 2026 from 22:00 to 23:00 local time, one minute at a time. As given data: 24 lanes, all booked and paid until 23:00; the alley opens at noon and closes at 23:00 every day. Once a minute, on the minute, the lane controller asks the booking database whether each lane is paid; a lane with no answer is marked unpaid and switched off, as built. The clocks went back on Sunday 25 October, so tonight local time equals UTC; in summer it runs an hour ahead. With no window chosen, the provider assigned Saturday 22:30 UTC. A required operating-system update, apply date Monday 26 October 2026, starts one minute into the window and takes the only copy offline for 9 minutes. A zone, as in Lost in the Cloud, is one of the provider's buildings; a standby copy sits in a second one. With a standby, the order follows the provider's page: the standby is updated first while the main copy answers, then the provider switches over to it (here at 22:40:10, for 40 seconds, between two checks), then the old main copy is updated. Updates "off" stops optional updates only. Another provider, with no window chosen, picked Saturday 22:10 UTC at random in this story. A 20-minute update is there to test the keep-last rule. Own server: no provider window, and the alley owns the chores.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play as built: dark from 22:31 to 22:40, 9 minutes, 216 lane-minutes marked unpaid. Switch the season to summer: the same update lands at 23:31 local, after closing, 0 dark. Set updates to "off": still 9 minutes dark. Turn on the standby copy: a 40-second switch-over between checks, 0 dark. Set the lane rule to keep the last confirmed booking: 9 minutes kept, 0 dark; then make the update 20 minutes: kept 15, dark 5. Try another provider's window: dark 22:11 to 22:20. Run it on our own server: 0 dark, and 5 chores. Then the fix: window chosen for Tuesday 10:00 UTC, standby on, notices to the shared inbox, keep the last booking.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the alley broke. Nobody had chosen a maintenance window, so the provider picked Saturday 22:30 UTC at random; a required operating-system update past its apply date took the only copy offline from 22:31 to 22:40, and the controller counted "no answer" as "unpaid": 24 lanes dark for 9 minutes. All summer, the same window had fallen at 23:30 local, after closing.

steps.title: A lane's paid check, and what "no answer" meant.
steps.text: Each minute the lane controller asks the booking database one question per lane: is it paid? A yes keeps the pinsetter and screen on. A no switches them off, which is right. What can go wrong is the third case: no answer at all. Tonight the controller treated "cannot check" exactly like "unpaid", a default nobody chose, so a database that was only offline looked like 24 lanes that had stopped paying. The Breaker Box met the same question: when something you depend on fails, decide in advance what you do instead, a fallback. Here a sensible fallback is to keep the last confirmed booking for a while: the lane was paid a minute ago and the league booked it until 23:00. The limit is the point of it. Keep it for up to 15 minutes, and a lane whose booking really ended gets a few free frames at worst; an outage longer than 15 minutes still goes dark, as the sim's 20-minute update shows (kept 15, dark 5).

steps.title: The maintenance window, step by step.
steps.text: First the window is chosen or assigned. Amazon's database service, for example, assigns a 30-minute window picked at random from an 8-hour block for each region, 22:00 to 06:00 UTC for London, on a random day: here, Saturday 22:30 UTC. Next comes the notice; what can go wrong is where it goes, and tonight's went to an address nobody reads. A required update carries an apply date, Monday 26 October 2026 here. After that date it runs in the next window, and switching updates off doesn't stop it. Last, the update itself: about 9 minutes with the only copy offline, from 22:31 to 22:40. The window is set in UTC, but the alley lives on local time. The two earlier required updates, Saturday 20 September 2025 and Saturday 13 June 2026, came while the clocks were an hour ahead, so they ran at 23:31 local, after the 23:00 closing, and no required update landed in the winter between. The clocks went back on Sunday 25 October, and the same window slid into league night.

steps.title: A standby in a second zone: an update becomes a short switch-over.
steps.text: Lost in the Cloud showed zones: separate buildings in one region, so one can fail without the other. A standby copy in a second zone is kept up to date with every write. For an operating-system update the provider works in three steps: update the standby while the main copy answers; switch the booking system over to the standby, which on Amazon's page typically takes less than a minute; then update the old main copy, which becomes the new standby. In the sim the switch-over takes 40 seconds and falls between two checks, so no lane misses a paid answer. What can still go wrong: a switch-over can land on a check, which the keep-last rule covers, and an upgrade of the database's own main program, its engine version, takes both copies down at once, so a quiet window still matters. A standby also costs money every month, and every write waits for the second copy.

steps.title: Managed or self-hosted: what you buy, what stays yours, and how hard it is to leave.
steps.text: A managed database buys you the chores: updates applied, spare copies kept, a switch-over built and tested by people who do it all day. What stays yours is everything the provider can't guess: its settings (the window, a standby), its notices (an inbox someone reads) and your exit plan. Self-hosting on a back-office server gives you every moment of downtime and every chore with it: updates, backups, failover and the 3 AM disk alarm. That swaps vendor risk, depending on a company you don't run, for staff risk, depending on people you may not have. Moving to another provider meets the same windows under new defaults, and pays for the move: exports, new connection details, testing. That cost of leaving is lock-in. Limit it with an exit plan: regular exports in a standard format, a database engine more than one provider runs, and a written note of what a move would take. Restarting the lane controllers faster is no fix either: they were never the part that failed. LATENT's a9e06, The Wrong Tool, asks the same build-or-buy question of AI.

steps.title: The walk into the provider's building.
steps.text: Everything Pegeen could touch was fine: the lanes, Elffin's pinsetters, the controller doing exactly what it was built to do. The cause lived in a building none of them had stood in, near London, where a provider's calendar said Saturday 22:30 UTC and had said so for fourteen months, harmlessly, while the clocks ran an hour ahead. After the last team had gone, Pegeen sat at the desk with the provider's page open and read it as a timetable: a window nobody chose, a notice sent to a closed mailbox, one copy in one building, and a clock that had moved the whole arrangement half an hour into league night.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for next Saturday. The lane controller asks the main copy of the booking database, in zone A, whether each lane is paid, once a minute, and keeps a lane on its last confirmed booking for up to 15 minutes if no answer comes. The main copy copies every write to a standby copy in zone B. Below: the maintenance window, chosen for Tuesday 10:00 UTC, before the noon opening, applies to both copies; the provider's notices go to the duty managers' shared inbox.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for next Saturday. The controller still asks once a minute, but a lane with no answer keeps its last confirmed booking for up to 15 minutes. The database has a standby copy in a second zone, so an operating-system update becomes a switch-over of under a minute. The window is chosen for Tuesday 10:00 UTC, 10:00 local in winter and 11:00 in summer, before the noon opening, and notices go to an inbox someone reads every shift. In the sim: 0 minutes dark on league night.

fix.title: The fix: keep the managed database, and take back its settings, its notices and the lanes' fallback
fix.text: Choose the maintenance window instead of accepting the assigned one: Tuesday 10:00 UTC, which is 10:00 local in winter and 11:00 in summer, both before the noon opening, and write down that the window is in UTC so the next person checks it against both clocks. Add a standby copy in a second zone, so an operating-system update or a failed building becomes a switch-over of under a minute instead of 9 minutes offline. Send the provider's notices to the duty managers' shared inbox, and make reading them part of every shift: a notice with an apply date is a job with a deadline. Change the lane rule: when the check gets no answer, keep the last confirmed booking for up to 15 minutes, then switch off. Keep a short exit plan beside the settings: where the exports go, which database engine it is, and what a move would take. Re-check the window whenever the opening hours change.

limits: Keep-last is a fallback with a hole on purpose: for up to 15 minutes a lane whose booking really ended can keep bowling free, and an outage longer than 15 minutes still goes dark (in the sim, a 20-minute update: kept 15, dark 5).

A standby covers operating-system updates and a failed zone, not everything: an upgrade to a new engine version takes both copies down together, so the chosen window and the keep-last rule still matter, and a second copy costs money every month.

How the provider sends notices, and to which address, is this story's provider's behaviour; the page read for this case describes the window, apply dates and the switch-over, not email. Check where your own provider's notices go before you assume anyone reads them.

explain.seniorTake: Buying a managed service buys the work, not the decisions. The provider will update, copy and switch over for you, on its calendar and in its clock, using whatever settings you left it with; the defaults are chosen to be safe for the provider's whole fleet, not quiet for your Saturday. So read the defaults as decisions somebody else made for you: the window, the number of copies, where notices go, and what your own system does when the service doesn't answer. Write those four down, check the window against both your summer and winter clocks, and keep an exit plan so leaving stays possible. Self-hosting is the honest alternative when you have the people for it; for most small teams, managed with its settings taken back is the stronger choice.

realWorld.title: Amazon RDS: a window picked at random
realWorld.text: The "Maintaining a DB instance" page says: "The 30-minute maintenance window is selected at random from an 8-hour block of time per region. If you don't specify a maintenance window when you create the DB instance, RDS assigns a 30-minute maintenance window on a randomly selected day of the week." Its table gives Europe (London), eu-west-2, the block from 22:00 to 06:00 UTC.

realWorld.title: Amazon RDS: required updates have an apply date
realWorld.text: On operating-system updates the page says: "A mandatory update is required and has an apply date. Plan to schedule your update before this apply date. After the specified apply date, Amazon RDS automatically upgrades the operating system for your DB instance to the latest version during one of your assigned maintenance windows." It adds: "Typically, the updates take about 10 minutes."

realWorld.title: Amazon RDS: moving the window won't dodge it
realWorld.text: "If you repeatedly modify your DB instance maintenance window to avoid a pending mandatory upgrade, Amazon RDS can still apply the upgrade outside of your preferred maintenance window after the mandatory apply date has passed." And for a required item: "The maintenance action will be applied to the resource and can't be deferred indefinitely."

realWorld.title: Amazon RDS: choose the quiet time
realWorld.text: "The maintenance window should fall at the time of lowest usage and thus might need modification from time to time." The window is set in UTC, so lowest usage has to be checked against local summer and winter time.

realWorld.title: Amazon RDS: the standby is updated first
realWorld.text: For Multi-AZ deployments the page lists the steps for operating-system updates: "Perform maintenance on the standby.", "Promote the standby to primary.", "Perform maintenance on the old primary, which becomes the new standby." And: "If there are underlying operating system patches that need to be applied, a short Multi-AZ failover is required to apply the patches to the primary DB instance. This failover typically lasts less than a minute."

realWorld.title: Amazon RDS: engine upgrades take both copies down
realWorld.text: "If you upgrade the database engine for your DB instance in a Multi-AZ deployment, Amazon RDS modifies both primary and secondary DB instances at the same time. In this case, both the primary and secondary DB instances in the Multi-AZ deployment are unavailable during the upgrade." That is why this story uses an operating-system update, and why the window still matters with a standby.

realWorld.title: Amazon RDS: a standby in a different zone
realWorld.text: The Multi-AZ page says: "In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, Amazon RDS automatically provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone." It also notes such deployments "can have increased write and commit latency compared to a Single-AZ deployment".

realWorld.title: GOV.UK: when the clocks change
realWorld.text: GOV.UK says the clocks go "back 1 hour at 2am on the last Sunday in October", and gives 25 October for 2026. "The period when the clocks are 1 hour ahead is called British Summer Time (BST)." A window set in UTC moves an hour on the alley's clock twice a year.

asked: What does a managed service still leave to you?
How do you limit vendor lock-in?
interview.answer: For most teams I'd start managed: the provider applies updates, keeps backups and runs the switch-over to a standby, work that is easy to get wrong and needs someone awake at 3 AM. I'd self-host only with a reason, such as a rule about where data lives or a feature no provider offers, and with the people to own updates, backups, failover and the alarms. Managed still leaves me four decisions. The maintenance window: choose the quietest hour, remembering it is set in UTC, and check it against summer and winter local time. The copies: one copy means every required update is downtime; a standby in a second zone turns an operating-system update into a short switch-over, though an engine upgrade still takes both down. The notices: required updates have apply dates, so notices go to a shared inbox someone reads. And my own system's fallback when the database doesn't answer, so 'cannot check' isn't treated as 'no'. On lock-in: keep an exit plan, regular exports in a standard format, a database engine more than one provider runs, and a written note of what a move would take, so leaving stays a choice. I'd tell the story of a bowling alley whose lanes went dark on league night because a window nobody chose slid into opening hours when the clocks went back.

atWork: A managed database left on its default settings is a common pattern: it works for months, then a window nobody chose meets a busy hour. List every managed service you depend on, and for each write down four things. When is its maintenance window, who chose it, and what is that in local time in both summer and winter? How many copies answer during an update: one, or a standby in a second zone? Where do the provider's notices go, and does someone read that inbox every week, with apply dates treated as deadlines? And what does your own code do when the service doesn't answer: does it treat "cannot check" as "no", or does it have a fallback with a limit? Then write a short exit plan: where regular exports go, in what format, and what a move would take. On AWS, the RDS console's maintenance section shows each instance's window and any pending required updates. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, controls A.5.23 (information security for use of cloud services), A.5.19 to A.5.22 (suppliers) and A.8.14 (redundancy) are where an auditor would look for these settings, the supplier's notices and the exit plan; if it is pursuing SOC 2, criterion CC9.2 covers risk from vendors and business partners. Build these in from the first design rather than at audit time. This case names those standards; it does not teach them.

recall.prompt: Your company's web shop keeps its orders in a managed database that a contractor created two years ago, with every setting left as it came. Every few months, at 21:40 on a Wednesday evening your time, checkout fails for about ten minutes, and nobody on the team has ever seen a warning. What is probably happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The provider's assigned maintenance window lands in busy hours, and a required update takes the only copy offline
Choose the window yourself for the quietest hour, and send the provider's notices to a shared inbox someone reads
Add a standby copy in a second zone, so an operating-system update becomes a short switch-over

recall.model: Almost certainly the database's maintenance window. Nobody chose one, so the provider assigned a weekly half hour at random, and it falls on a busy Wednesday evening. Every few months a required update with an apply date runs in that window and takes the only copy offline for about ten minutes; its notices go to whatever address the contractor used, so nobody sees them. I'd choose the window myself for the quietest hour, checking it in local summer and winter time, and send the provider's notices to a shared inbox someone reads. I'd add a standby copy in a second zone, so an operating-system update becomes a switch-over of under a minute instead of ten minutes offline. And I'd give checkout a fallback for the minute it can't reach the database, rather than failing every order.

recall.prompt: In the sim, as built on 31 October 2026 (winter, the provider's assigned window, one copy, no answer counts as unpaid), which one change keeps all 24 lanes lit from 22:00 to 23:00 while the update still starts at 22:31 local?
options: Standby copy in a second zone
recall.why: With a standby the update still starts at 22:31, but the standby is updated first while the main copy answers, then a 40-second switch-over falls between two checks: 0 minutes dark. Updates "off" changes nothing: the update is required and past its apply date, 9 minutes dark. Summer keeps the lanes lit only because the update moves to 23:31 local, after closing. Another provider's window is dark from 22:11 to 22:20.

recall.prompt: According to Amazon RDS's "Maintaining a DB instance" page, what happens to a mandatory operating-system update after its apply date?
options: It is cancelled unless someone approves it
RDS applies it automatically during one of your assigned maintenance windows
It waits until updates are switched back on
It runs at once, outside any window, the moment the date passes
recall.why: The page says: "After the specified apply date, Amazon RDS automatically upgrades the operating system for your DB instance to the latest version during one of your assigned maintenance windows." That is why switching updates off didn't save league night.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: should we run our database as a managed service or host it ourselves, and what does a managed service still leave to us?

keyIdeas.idea: Managed hands over the chores: applying updates, backups and the failover machinery
What stays yours: its settings (the window, the copies), reading its notices, and an exit plan
Self-hosting gives control of downtime but swaps vendor risk for staff risk: on-call, disk alarms, your own failover

recall.model: For most teams I'd choose managed: the provider does the chores, applying updates, taking backups and running the failover to a standby, and does them better than a small team would. Managed still leaves us the decisions: its settings, such as the maintenance window (chosen for our quietest hour, in UTC, checked against summer and winter) and how many copies answer during an update; its notices, which carry apply dates and need an inbox someone reads; and an exit plan, so leaving stays possible. Hosting it ourselves gives us control of every moment of downtime, but swaps vendor risk for staff risk: someone on call for the 3 AM disk alarm, our own backups to test, our own failover to build. I'd do that only with the people for it and a reason the provider can't meet.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Every Saturday since has been clean: the window is Tuesday 10:00, there's a standby in a second zone, notices go to our shared inbox, and lanes keep their last confirmed booking for up to 15 minutes. In February we started opening at 10:00 on weekdays for school groups. In the shared inbox was a notice: a required upgrade of the database's main program to a new version, apply date Monday 1 March 2027. We read it and thought the standby had us covered. On Tuesday 2 March 2027 at 10:01, mid-game, the provider's page shows the main copy and the standby being upgraded together, 10:01 to 10:21. The lanes kept their 10:00 bookings until 10:15, then all 24 went dark from 10:16 to 10:21: 5 minutes, 120 lane-minutes marked unpaid, with a school group in every lane.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the standby not keep the lanes lit, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: An engine-version upgrade takes both copies down at once; a standby only covers operating-system updates and a failed zone
The window must move when the opening hours change: re-pick it for the new quietest hour
Plan the upgrade on purpose: schedule or apply it before the apply date at a closed hour, after testing it

coldCase.model: This one was an engine version upgrade, a new version of the database's main program, and the provider upgrades both copies at the same time for those, so the standby couldn't take over: there was nothing left answering for 20 minutes. Keep-last covered the first 15 and then ran out, which is exactly its limit. Two things changed under the fix: the update was a different kind, and the opening hours moved, so a Tuesday 10:00 window that was quiet in November now sits in school bowling. Move the window to the new quietest hour, before opening or after closing, in UTC and checked against summer time too, and re-check it whenever the hours change. And plan the upgrade on purpose: when a notice like this lands, test the upgrade on a copy first, then schedule it, or apply it early, at a closed hour before the apply date, rather than letting it take the next window.
